title: Sport Skills and Physical Preparation: Why Athletes Need Both
description: Sport skills and physical preparation work together. WSP explains how strength, speed, mobility, and year-round training support athletic performance.
author: Ben Bershad
alt: College athletes walking toward the camera while performing knee-hug stretches on the turf inside Warrior Sports Performance
bodyHtml:
Another tournament. Another clinic. Another opportunity to get more reps.

The message to athletes and parents can feel constant: if you want to improve, you need to play more. More games, more practices, more private lessons, more showcases. My concern with that message is what can get squeezed out of the schedule - the work that helps prepare the body to perform.

Skill matters - a lacrosse player needs stick work. A soccer player needs touches on the ball. A swimmer needs time developing technique in the water. Strength training cannot replace those things.

But knowing what to do and having the physical capacity to do it are connected. Athletes also need to produce force, move quickly, control their bodies, and recover from the demands of their sport. A complete development plan makes room for both.

At WSP, we recommend strength training two to three times per week during the off-season and once per week during the sport season. That is our starting point, with the training adjusted to the athlete’s age, experience, practice and game schedule, and recovery. The goal is simple: keep developing your sport skills while building and maintaining the body you need to use them.

Practicing your sport and preparing your body have different jobs

Skill practice develops technique, timing, decision-making, and the ability to respond to a real opponent or competitive situation. You learn those things by practicing and playing your sport.

Physical preparation focuses on the qualities that support that performance: strength, power, speed, conditioning, and control through useful ranges of motion. There is overlap—sport practice is physical—but playing more does not automatically address every physical need.

Think about a player trying to create space. Recognizing the opening is one task. Accelerating into it is another. Slowing down, changing direction, and accelerating again add further demands. The decision and the movement have to work together.

In the gym and on the training floor, we can break those physical tasks down, coach them, and gradually increase the challenge. Sport practice then gives the athlete opportunities to apply those qualities in context.

Research supports adding physical preparation to sport practice

A systematic review by Lesinski and colleagues examined 43 studies of young athletes. Importantly, the comparison groups continued their regular sport training. Adding resistance training produced improvements in strength and jumping, with smaller benefits in sprinting, agility tests, and sport-specific performance measures. [1]

That matters because the comparison was not simply active kids versus inactive kids. It supports the idea that athletes who already practice can still benefit from structured physical preparation.

It also keeps our expectations honest. A better strength test or faster planned change-of-direction drill does not automatically mean better decisions during a game. Athletes still need coaching and practice in their sport. The two types of work support different parts of development.

Strength, acceleration, deceleration, change of direction, mobility, and core work need a purpose

Being fast is useful. Being able to slow down under control and move again is also important. That is why I want athletes to practice both producing movement and controlling it.

Depending on the athlete, that might include strength exercises, short accelerations, landing practice, and progressively faster stopping or direction-change tasks. The goal is to connect the physical qualities—not turn every session into an exhausting circuit.

Mobility work should address the movement the athlete needs, with control through the available range. Core work should have a clear purpose too, such as maintaining trunk position or controlling rotation. It does not have to mean an endless list of stretches and sit-ups.

These are coaching tools, not separate guarantees against injury. We choose them according to the athlete’s needs and fit them into the whole program.

What about the athlete practicing or playing five days a week?

Consider an athlete whose week includes five days of practices and games, with no planned strength work, mobility work, or trunk training. That athlete is working hard. The question is whether the schedule is developing everything they need.

Before deciding something is missing, we should ask what the team already includes. Some coaches build physical preparation into practice and warm-ups. It counts, even if it does not happen in a separate gym session.

If those needs truly are being missed, the answer is not automatically to add two more hard days. It may mean replacing an optional session, coordinating with the sport coach, or incorporating a short, purposeful strength session into an existing training day while preserving recovery.

The IOC’s youth-development consensus recommends balancing athletic development with regular rest, recovery, and the athlete’s other needs. It is expert guidance rather than proof of one ideal schedule, but it supports looking beyond the number of practices on the calendar. [2]

My question for families is simple: before signing up for another opportunity, what does this athlete need most right now?

Take care of the body throughout the year

Physical preparation should change with the season. An off-season may allow more time to build strength and develop movement skills. During competition, we can adjust the amount of work to support performance and preserve what the athlete has built. Recovery periods belong in that plan too.

In a small study of 14 male professional soccer players, one weekly strength session maintained preseason strength and sprint gains over 12 in-season weeks, while training every other week did not maintain those gains. That was a performance study, not an injury study, and it does not establish a universal weekly prescription. It illustrates why strength work should not automatically disappear when games begin. [3]

Year-round attention does not mean year-round hard training. It means having a plan for building, maintaining, and recovering instead of treating physical preparation as something we only address when there is a problem.

Being available is part of being able to perform. Keeping physical preparation in the plan during the season can help athletes maintain strength and support the demands of their sport, although no program can guarantee an injury-free season. To learn more, read our article, Why In-Season Strength Training Matters for Athletes.

Build the athlete and keep developing the skill

At Warrior Sports Performance, I want our work to complement what athletes are learning from their sport coaches. The aim is to help them become physically better prepared to use those skills.

That starts with understanding the whole week: practices, games, other training, and recovery. From there, we can decide what the athlete needs and where it fits.

Keep practicing the skills your sport demands. Give your body the preparation to support them.

If you would like help finding that balance, contact Warrior Sports Performance in Norfolk, MA, at info@warriorsportsperformance.com. Bring us the athlete’s schedule and goals, and we can talk through a practical plan.

Research referenced

[1] Lesinski M, Prieske O, Granacher U. Effects and dose–response relationships of resistance training on physical performance in youth athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2016;50(13):781–795. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2015-095497.

[2] Bergeron MF, et al. International Olympic Committee consensus statement on youth athletic development. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2015;49(13):843–851. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2015-094962.

[3] Rønnestad BR, Nymark BS, Raastad T. Effects of in-season strength maintenance training frequency in professional soccer players. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2011;25(10):2653–2660. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e31822dcd96.

title: Why In-Season Strength Training Matters for Athletes
description: Why strength training belongs in the season—and how to fit it around practices, games, and recovery.
author: Ben Bershad
alt: Athlete performing a trap-bar deadlift at Warrior Sports Performance
paragraphs: Once the season starts, the schedule fills up quickly. Between practices, games, school, and travel, it is easy to let strength training fall off the calendar.

My view is simple: the strength an athlete worked to build before the season is worth maintaining during it. That does not mean adding hard workouts just to do more. It means keeping an appropriate amount of purposeful strength work in the week.

There are two reasons to make room for it: maintaining physical qualities that support performance, and helping reduce certain injury risks. Neither requires us to promise that training will make an athlete injury-proof.
Keep the strength you worked to build
Playing a sport and training for strength are different demands. Practices and games do not necessarily provide the same stimulus as a planned strength session.

In a small study of 14 male professional soccer players, Rønnestad and colleagues compared strength training once a week with once every two weeks during the first 12 weeks of the season. The weekly group maintained its preseason gains in strength and sprint performance; the every-other-week group lost ground in those measures. [1]

That study measured performance, not injuries, and professional soccer players are not the same population as every young athlete we coach. Still, it gives us a useful example of how a modest, consistent training commitment can help maintain strength during a season. It does not establish one session a week as the right prescription for everyone.
What does the research say about injury risk?

One useful example comes from Petersen and colleagues. They studied 942 male soccer players across 50 teams. The intervention group completed a progressive 10-week Nordic hamstring exercise program, followed by weekly training during the season. The comparison group followed its usual training. Researchers recorded 15 acute hamstring injuries in the intervention group versus 52 in the comparison group. [2]

That is evidence for a particular strengthening program and a particular injury outcome. Because the program included both a build-up phase and ongoing seasonal work, we cannot credit the in-season portion alone. We also cannot assume that any gym workout will produce the same result in every sport.

The broader research supports taking strength work seriously. A 2018 systematic review and meta-analysis by Lauersen and colleagues included six studies with 7,738 participants and found fewer injuries in the strength-based intervention groups. The programs, populations, and injuries differed, so the finding is not a universal prediction for an individual athlete. [3]
Reducing risk is different from eliminating it
We cannot prevent every awkward landing, collision, or unexpected moment in sport. No honest training program can guarantee an injury-free season.

The aim is to help athletes stay physically prepared for the demands they face. Maintaining muscular strength is one part of that preparation. The studies above support structured training programs; they do not prove that stronger muscles, by themselves, explain every reduction in injury risk.
That is why I would rather talk about helping reduce risk than promising to prevent injuries. Training should also account for the athlete’s practice load, recovery, and any existing injury.
In-season training should fit the season

At Warrior Sports Performance, my approach is to look at the athlete’s whole week before deciding what belongs in a session. A week with several games calls for a different decision from a lighter week.

That can mean doing fewer sets, keeping familiar exercises, or adjusting when the session takes place. We can keep the work meaningful without making soreness or exhaustion the goal. A busy athlete needs a manageable plan, not another competition in the weight room.

A player who has been lifting regularly can build on that experience. An athlete who is new to strength training needs a gradual starting point, even if the season is already underway. Persistent pain or an existing injury calls for appropriate assessment and coordination with the athlete’s healthcare professional.
Consistency matters more than a complicated workout

The practical message for athletes and parents is to keep strength training in the conversation when the season begins. Talk with your coaches about where it fits, what needs to be maintained, and how to adjust it as the schedule changes.
You do not need to chase personal records every week. You need a clear reason for the work and an amount the athlete can recover from.

If you would like help building an in-season training plan, contact Warrior Sports Performance in Norfolk, MA, at info@warriorsportsperformance.com. Bring us the practice and game schedule, and we can talk through a practical starting point.
Research referenced

[1] Rønnestad BR, Nymark BS, Raastad T. Effects of in-season strength maintenance training frequency in professional soccer players. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2011;25(10):2653–2660.

[2] Petersen J, Thorborg K, Nielsen MB, Budtz-Jørgensen E, Hölmich P. Preventive effect of eccentric training on acute hamstring injuries in men’s soccer: a cluster-randomized controlled trial. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2011;39(11):2296–2303.

[3] Lauersen JB, Andersen TE, Andersen LB. Strength training as superior, dose-dependent and safe prevention of acute and overuse sports injuries: a systematic review, qualitative analysis and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;52:1557–1563.
